# Orrin Windmill Miller's Book

## Working the mill

- The Orrin mill is set to the wind at first light by turning the cap with the tail pole, and the miller sets the sails to four cloths on each stock when the wind is below 20 knots by the flag on the church. A fifth cloth is added only when the wind drops to a steady breeze, and all cloths are taken in again at once if the flag stands straight out, because a sail caught in a gust with full canvas can tear the stock from the windshaft. The brake is always applied before anyone goes up the sails, and the miller shouts the word brake aloud and waits for the answer from the stone floor before he leaves the cap.
- The runner stone at Orrin is dressed every 11 days of grinding, and the dressing takes a full morning with the mill stopped and the stone lifted on the crane. The miller cuts the furrows fresh with the mill bill and tests the face with the paint staff, a staff daubed with red ochre that marks the high spots when drawn across the stone. A stone dressed too deep wastes the grain and heats the meal, while one left too long makes coarse flour that the bakers send back and for which the mill must give credit against the next load.
- Wheat is ground to a fineness that must pass the 60 mesh sifter for white bread flour, and anything left in the sifter is returned to the hopper for a second grinding. The miller samples the meal between finger and thumb every quarter hour, listening to the stones as much as feeling the flour, and a squealing stone is a stone running dry which is stopped at once. Barley for the brewery is ground coarser and never sifted, and it is sacked in the grey sacks so it cannot be mistaken for bakers' flour in the dark of the sack loft.
- The toll taken by the Orrin miller is one sixteenth of the grain by measure, as it has been since the charter, and the toll dish hangs from a nail by the hopper where any customer can see it filled. The miller may not take toll from the poor of the parish and writes their names in the book on the lintel each Michaelmas. Disputes about short weight are settled by weighing the sack on the beam scales in front of the customer and the parish clerk, and a miller found short twice in a year loses his licence at the next court.
- The sack hoist is greased every Saturday evening with tallow from the pot on the stone floor, and the greasing is the last job before the mill is shut for Sunday. The hoist chain is run out to its full length and examined link by link, and any link that shows a bright worn patch is marked with a nick of the file and reported to the smith at Tuesday's market. Nobody rides the hoist with a sack, whatever the hurry of the morning, and the trap doors are closed behind every lift so a visitor does not walk into the opening in the half dark.
